title: Understanding Email Encryption (2025)
author: jon128
content_excerpt:
Google Mail's $5/seat offering is the first one that comes to mind.

  04 May 2011
  Starting with Chrome 13, we'll have HTTPS pins for most Google properties. This means that certificate chains for, say, https://www.google.com, must include a whitelisted public key. It's a fatal error otherwise. 

  https://www.imperialviolet.org/2011/05/04/pinning.html
ImperialViolet is Adam Langley’s personal technical blog. Langley worked at Google on HTTPS infrastructure and Chrome’s SSL stack.

A Tauri app, which is essentially a Chromium browser instance with no address bar and widgets to access browser settings, a Fastmail desktop "app" made with Tauri can potentially even the playing field between Google the Goliath and Fastmail the David on the TLS certificate pinning front. Tauri is like Electron but sucks a lot less.

  https://tauri.app/
_

> if you've spending tens of thousands of dollars per month

Such as, 8,000 users at $40k/month for Google Mail.

Yubico has great volume discounts for a part of the CapEx side of a sane deployment of this.

The basic WebAuthn/FIDO2-only Yubikeys with a Fastmail logo on them would be, as the kids said a generation ago, "dope".

_

> where they have a Helpdesk

Quality attention to cicd and artifact release may avoid and potentially reduce conventional helpdesk activity.

For individual users of SaaS, provided the .dmg or .msi of the downstream Betterbird/Thunderbird (or other MUA) has sound cicd and decent release attention, no more additional support tickets than reasonable should occur beyond an initial phase.

A downstream MUA distro can eliminate manual configuration and superfluous details, such as the shit experience with Thunderbird on macOS (Thunderbird's fault 100%) with Oath2 I saw in the last few months. Such a distro could be tuned with a slew of relatively small adjustments reducing existing support ticket traffic.

Startups with headcount of 20 to 30, a good chunk of that being developers, where I have historically preferred to dwell, helpdesk is not there nor wanted for. Higher quality customers are here.

_

> and golden image deploys

Chromebooks, which not including K-12 did outnumber macOS in non-personal environments around a half-decade ago during that Event 201 thing. Super low IT overhead with those.

I have been distant from MIS type of IT for a while but have heard echoes or binocular'd in a bit and believe the golden image era has quietly passed us.

Conventional image pattern shouldn't be necessary anywhere now.

Somewhere in 2019, Apple warped native tooling in tandem with device firmware behavior to squeeze out the conventional image pattern ; killed it off.

Apple Business now includes built-in mobile device management which can enroll and set up Apple devices then apply standard settings and apps through "Blueprints" ; the .dmg would be trivial to push out. The successor to Jamf.

With Microsoft Intune, propagation of .msi packages to enrolled devices is a day-to-day task.

Ubuntu, RedHat, SuSE, Qubes, and all related distros, when under IT teams that can code on a rudimentary level, are managed with Ansible or Salt, without the "enterprise tax" part.

What all of these have in common is centralized org-wide device management where the ability to push out a .msi or .dmg or .deb/.rpm/.AppImage is there.

In similar spirit to certificate pinning, the advanced customers have dedicated private cicd consume source code from the OS vendor.

The more advanced are on

  Bootstrappable builds: how and why
  https://lwn.net/Articles/1088279/
which in tandem with cryptography-grade hashes, has over half way solved the "Trusting Trust" problem that Ken Thompson raised.

_

> what other SaaS consumer products use certificate pinning.

Slack has the low-hanging-fruit opportunity to with their Electron app, but has reportedly dropped the ball. This is great for tech workers who like to divert all Slack contents to a separate local data sink for archiving and discovery and non-shitty data access.

This repo from about seven years ago looks abandoned and inactive, but

  https://github.com/myxious/electron-root-ssl-pinning
was not necessary for anyone who wanted to do it.

_

> let's expand it to banks and government departments in most countries.

With the episodic exposure I had with computer vision -> flow chart startups in the SF Bay Area many years ago, relatively ongoing time sinks with some archetypal MBA twat types, and some perceived legendary tier banks running on one of the two legit clouds (neither of which is that Azure garbage), who then fell on customer-facing downtime by not deploying with rudimentary cloud patterns that startups don't fail to do (as we recently found out), I am left feeling not confident that banks can do IT with self-reliance these days.

They can still push out .msi and group policy objects though, for sure.

From anecdotes I hear of and distant observations of state governments, departments of the big federal government sans some of the cooler TLA, and govs in Europe, I am not optimistic about those.

About a decade and a half ago we used to look at these two types of institutions and go "ah, the big guys, in their big buildings, they broker a thing I need, with their marble floors and reassuring smiles, these egregore have got it all figured out".

As a staff level DevOps / DevSecOps / whatever who has been along for the ride with a share of Silicon Valley culture-OS startups with enterprise customers, closely followed practices and white papers of hyperscalers and elite security firms, thus can see through an

title: OccupySaaS
author: jongjong
content_excerpt:
IMO, the real reason they were laid off is because our economic system is broken. It's wealth concentration for those in the center of the scheme and deprivation for those in the periphery.

Rapid technological improvement is just a convenient justification for letting people go. It sounds a lot better than the real explanation "The system is broken and we need to keep optimizing money flows to sustain the scheme to prevent hyperinflation." The system destroys value faster than technology can create it; which is quite an impressive feat because technology opens up massive capabilities but look at reality; AI is being massively misallocated.

Mark my words; the business model for AI, if the current trends continue, isn't going to be about "robots making everyone's lives better"; it's going to be about "AI agents which patch vulnerabilities that AI agents themselves created."

This is the reality we're heading into. No amount of incredible technology is going to solve that problem if it follows the rules of the current economic system. That's what the incentives lead to.

title: OccupySaaS
author: nrawe
content_excerpt:
I get the anger; I think this is misguided. I know this will be distinctly unpopular (bye-bye karma!)

SWEs in general have been paid significantly higher salaries for decades in part because of the skill level needed and that they are generally working on capital projects (build new thing) vs operational projects (maintain thing built). It's the difference between needing a Landscaper to come in a completely reshape a bit of land for £10k once, and Gardener to come in a mow/prune once a week for £10. Most salaried SWEs don't necessarily see that every project they work on is a new patch of land to be landscaped; those who've contracted do.

SWEs have been effectively paid this "danger money" because of that inherent volatility in projects being shut down, which has been there since the dot com bubble but is now amplified because of the relative size of the tech sector.

The skills barrier which has been eroded in part by the lack of professional standards (anyone who can edit a PHP script can call themselves an SWE vs a Chartered Accountant which has to be certified), and now explicitly because of AI.

In some ways this just looks like "FOSS for Angry Millennials" without the understanding of the further damage that this will do to them and their industry. These are the forces its trying to get revenge for: (a) high inflationary creating risky environments for businesses to navigate, (b) tax changes which have impacted how organisations pay for SWEs, (c) AI offering "efficiencies" in all parts of the value chain, (d) the demand for ever-growing returns by shareholders as we enter the end-state of neoliberalism.

None of that is improved by this movement. Regardless of what you think of them, the original Occupy movement made it impossible for the people responsible for the crash to not be aware of/somewhat put out by those impacted by the crash. This is Just Another Open Source project. The way for those impacted is: (a) keep their skills sharp by helping charity projects that need the volunteer support; (b) get active politically on a local level; (c) use the time to start their own businesses with others.

There is a firmament that is needed on which all tech grows like Linux which is a good thing. This is not good for the Landscapers or the Gardeners, nor does it fix the issues which have led to the layoffs.

title: OccupySaaS
author: spwa4
content_excerpt:
> The whole reason to pay for software is to offload the liability to a 3rd-party. In simpler words: "As a company, I have this need and I don't want to solve it myself. Also, if I pay someone, I can sue them on contract breach just in case."

Ah management-style cover-your-ass engineering. Which doesn't work even with things like IBM contracts, never mind with anyone smaller. The problem is what they actually guarantee.

When you actually investigate the question (because you were a Google SRE and you move to a smaller company, and obviously disaster preparation starts with knowing what happens when disaster strikes): "Say, really smart manager, what does the contract actually say happens when you need the cover-your-ass provisions? Let's say AWS fails to give us machines. Let's say this software doesn't deliver. Let's say the bank connection we're paying for breaks". First observation: the managers (at a very big European telco) don't actually know the answer to this question. Or they pretend not to (I'm pretty sure they just lied to me, didn't care about anything but the checkmark, and did in fact know they did not have any option for disaster recovery because their developers had told them many times).

Answers: AWS doesn't give you a cent back, under any circumstances, does NOT get your servers back online but MAY give you 20% reduction on your future bill.

Software doesn't deliver, then we don't have to pay the last milestone payment (10% of the cost), and the supplier does nothing anymore.

If the bank connection breaks, nothing happens. You are forced to keep paying anyway. Although, I guess you get the transaction cost for free because there won't bee any transactions. I do hear there's a small problem with that.

So, obviously, no, this does not cover the company's ass at all. It's about a manager being able to say they very cheaply did something. What will happen to the company in case of actual problems? It'll immediately cease to function, and none of these cover-your-ass provisions will matter at all. Which is, of course, what happened about 4 months later and the company's new SREs were expected to fix the shit ASAP, without ANY help from the "service" part of these platforms. We had to buy new services to get it fixed, once the service was down senior management literally got involved and approved the purchase orders, yelled at a bunch of infrastructure teams to make changes they never would and the company never got the money back from the "guaranteed" platforms. It cost about 15x, for that year, what it would have cost to have 2 providers for the service, and I'm sure that more than covered a development team for the software. And thank god we at least hosted our own source and made sure local builds worked.

By the way: they just switched to the newly ordered much more expensive platform. About 3 weeks later, focus was moved away, by management, from repairing stuff and so the ability to switch back was ... just dropped.
